1:
Why a fresh command was needed at all is the first question. Ellicott answers that no provision had hitherto been made for keeping the passover in the wilderness, since but for the rebellion of the people the next passover after the Egyptian one would have fallen in Canaan, and it was for that one only that provision had been made. Gill says the same from the other side, that without a fresh precept, or an explanation of the former, the people might not have thought themselves obliged until they came into the land. Henry draws a large inference: the first institution appointed the feast for the land of promise, and no passover was kept after this one until they reached Canaan, which he takes as an early indication that the ceremonial institutions would at last be abolished, since so soon after they were appointed some were suffered to lie asleep for years together. Calvin reads the reminder as a reproach: we may infer how great was the carelessness, nay the ingratitude, of the people, from God's having to recall the passover to their memory before a year had elapsed, for what would they do fifty years hence if there was danger of their forgetting in so short a time? Had they been voluntarily assiduous it would have been needless to repeat what was enjoined already, and severely, with threats.

That the chapter stands out of its order all agree, and two explanations are offered. Wesley says the events fall in the first month and therefore before the numbering of the people, which was not until the second, but that the narrative is placed after it because of the special case about the passover which arose later. Clarke thinks the displacement mechanical rather than deliberate. The first fourteen verses belong with the transactions at the opening of the book, and transpositions of this kind are not hard to account for, since in very early times writing was on leaves of papyrus, so that entries were easily deranged and might be bound into a wrong place when a series was afterwards made into a book. He has handled such manuscripts himself, leaves pierced and strung on a cord, and says that if the cord breaks it is exceedingly difficult to restore each leaf to its place.

Of the keeping itself the notices are brief and the observations pointed. Gill dates it the fourteenth of Nisan, answering to part of our March, and Ellicott renders the hour as between the two evenings; on the phrase about rites and ceremonies Ellicott prefers statutes and ordinances, observing that since some directions given for the Egyptian passover could not be kept in the wilderness, the reference must be to those of permanent obligation. Henry marks two things in the obedience: Moses faithfully transmitted his orders, magistrates being bound to be monitors and ministers to stir up men's minds by way of remembrance; and the people, though they had lately kept the feast of dedication, did not plead that against this one, for extraordinary performances must not supersede stated services. That they kept it in a desert is the point he presses last — though our condition be solitary and unsettled we must keep up our attendance upon God by holy ordinances as we have opportunity. Calvin adds that their obedience is praised precisely because they neither added anything to nor diminished anything from God's command. Gill and Ellicott both notice what is missing, that nothing is said of the seven days of unleavened bread, and give the same reason: flour enough for so great a multitude for seven days would hardly be procurable in the wilderness, though enough for a single meal might be had from the neighbouring countries — Gill naming Midian, where Jethro lived, as near enough to Sinai to supply it.
6:
Who the defiled men were is a matter of conjecture, and Ellicott offers a good one. It has been supposed that they were Mishael and Elzaphan, who buried their cousins Nadab and Abihu about this time; and the dates fit, since if the consecration of Aaron and his sons began on the first day of the first month, and the deaths could not have fallen before the eighth, then a defilement lasting seven days would leave those who buried them unclean on the fourteenth. He offers it as one of the many undesigned coincidences with which Scripture abounds, and adds that no men would be so likely to bring this particular inquiry to Moses as those whom Moses himself had directed to carry out that burial. Clarke guesses more generally that the defilement came of assisting at somebody's burial, a work both of necessity and of mercy. Gill allows either that a whole household was defiled by a death among them, or that individuals had touched the body or been concerned in interring it, and he raises the question how the men knew they were unclean at all, since no such law stood in the first institution of the passover — answering from the tradition that the section about the red heifer and defilement by the dead was delivered on the day the tabernacle was erected, and so, though recorded later, was given out before this.

Their difficulty is a genuine collision of duties. Calvin states it exactly: the unclean were not permitted to approach the sacred feast, and yet it was sinful to neglect this exercise of religion, so that a kind of discrepancy arose between two commands. Wesley puts the same dilemma in the men's own mouths — if we neglect the offering we must be cut off, and if we keep it in these circumstances we must also be cut off; what shall we do? Keil records the answer given in the meantime, that Moses told them to stand while he heard what the Lord would command. Calvin makes much of that pause. Even Moses confessed himself perplexed and sought time to inquire of God, and the extraordinary modesty of the prophet displays itself in his not daring to pronounce on a doubtful matter although he was their lawgiver — by which he showed the more clearly that he had not given the Law out of his own head, since he did not dare so much as to interpret it without a fresh command.

What the answer did was to make an exception rather than to bend the rule. Calvin observes that God takes away the contradiction by a special provision, assigning the second month to those whom just necessity excused, and that the relief extends beyond the unclean to men absent on a journey, of whom the same question might be raised. He is careful about the limits of it: this was no concession to despisers, and the men themselves had complained of their own accord, from which we infer their pious solicitude. Clarke draws the same line and its consequence — the passover might on occasion be kept twice, but the man who had no legal hindrance and kept it at neither time was to be cut off, the reason given being that he brought not the offering of God in its appointed season; and since Christ our passover is sacrificed for us, those who do not sooner or later eat the true Passover will be cut off from the rest prepared for the people of God, and for that same reason. Ellicott closes on the type: the legal uncleanness that barred a man from the passover may be regarded as figuring the moral and spiritual unfitness that bars men from the Lord's Supper.
9:
The terms of the concession are precise, and one of its words has been suspected from antiquity. Keil gives the general instruction as covering everyone defiled by a corpse or upon a distant journey, of the men then living and of their future families alike, the second passover to be kept on the fourteenth of the second month between the two evenings and in all respects according to the statute of the feast — of which he names the three leading points, eating the lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, leaving nothing till the next day, and not breaking a bone. Both he and Ellicott stop at the word rendered afar off, which is one of the ten places in the Pentateuch where words carry the dots known as puncta extraordinaria. Ellicott reports the rabbinical explanation as an alternative: either the word is spurious, not being found where the same case is stated again a few verses later, or it is not to be taken in its literal signification but in a qualified sense. Keil favours the second and specifies it, that distance is reckoned from Jerusalem, or from the threshold of the outer court of the temple, citing the Mishnah for it. Wesley widens the two named cases rather than narrowing them: the Hebrews take these as instances under which other hindrances of like nature are comprehended, such as being kept back by disease or by uncleanness of another kind.

On the date and its keeping the notes are Gill's and Ellicott's. Gill names the month Ijar, answering to part of our April and part of our May, and reads the interval as deliberate provision: a month was allowed for the defiled to cleanse themselves and for those on a journey to return home and prepare, the feast being neither to be omitted altogether nor deferred any longer than that. It was to fall on the same day of the month and at the same time of day as the first, and he gives the reason — still the more to keep in mind the saving of their firstborn and their deliverance out of Egypt at that hour. Ellicott presses a point of grammar with a consequence attached: the word rendered ordinances is singular, according to all the ordinance, and its primary reference is probably to the law respecting the paschal lamb itself rather than to the whole festal week; and he notes that by Jewish tradition the second feast was observed for one day only instead of seven, so that it was not necessary to put away leaven.

The closing clauses set a penalty and open a door. Gill defines the clean man simply as one free from pollution by a dead body or the like, so that the threat falls on the man who had no hindrance at either season. Ellicott takes the sentence that he shall bear his sin in its severest sense, that he shall be put to death. Against that stands the provision for the stranger, which all three voices read as a genuine admission on terms. Gill holds that such a man must become a proselyte of righteousness and be circumcised, since otherwise he might not eat of the passover at all; and he passes on the Jewish reading of the clause, that Ben Gersom refers it to the second passover and to a proselyte who had not been obliged to the first, not being then a proselyte but becoming one between the two, with Aben Ezra understanding it of a second passover likewise, though he observes that some take the first to be meant. Ellicott simply refers the law respecting the stranger back to its fuller statement in the twelfth of Exodus, and Wesley glosses the word in one breath: a stranger, that is, one who is a proselyte.
15:
A new subject opens here, and Clarke thinks it ought to have opened a chapter: he cites Calmet, who held that this verse has no connection with what goes before and that the section begun here should run on to the end of the following account. Gill fixes the day as the first of the first month in the second year after the coming out of Egypt. What exactly the cloud covered is disputed. Ellicott renders the phrase the tabernacle belonging to the tent of the testimony and argues against confining the cloud to the innermost chamber where the two tables were kept: the older narrative says that Moses could not enter the tent of meeting because the cloud abode upon it, with no reference to any particular part of the structure, though he grants that it was from above the mercy-seat that the divine presence was specially manifested. Wesley takes the other side, glossing it as the tabernacle above the tent of the testimony, that is, the part in which the ark stood, for there the pillar rested.

That it was a standing miracle rather than a single wonder is the point several voices press. Keil insists the covering was constant, not a phenomenon that appeared when the dwelling was first reared and then vanished; and he explains the settling of the cloud by the fact that the tabernacle was taken to pieces for the march, so that the pillar, which ordinarily soared above the ark as it was carried in front of the army, visibly came down as a signal that the sanctuary was to be pitched there, and then rested upon it once it stood. Calvin meets the obvious objection, that the cloud had guided them like a banner ever since Egypt and so cannot first have begun to order their marches now. His answer is that a new fact is being related: the pillar which had hitherto hung in the air before the camp now settled on the sanctuary, a fresh acquisition of grace proclaimed by a more certain and conspicuous sign, as if God showed himself more closely and familiarly as their leader. Henry finds in the pairing of cloud and fire a demonstration that God kept them night and day, while the darkness of the one and the terror of the other suited a dispensation dimmer than the discovery since made of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

What the sign required was an obedience without a timetable. Henry presses it hardest: as long as the cloud rested they rested, though it were a month or a year, however much they longed to be pressing on toward Canaan — he that believeth does not make haste, and no time is lost while we are waiting God's time, it being as acceptable a submission to sit still contentedly when our lot requires it as to work when we are called to it. He finds the people's constant uncertainty deliberate, that they might be always ready to march on short warning, as we are kept uncertain of the hour of our own removal. Gill is careful about the phrase rendered the commandment: there was no command in form given, nor any audible voice heard, but the taking up of the cloud was interpretatively the order of God. Calvin grants that mouth stands by metonymy for speech and doubts whether God actually spoke, yet holds that the name of speech was rightly given to the sign, since God speaks as much to the eyes by outward signs as to the ears by His voice — from which he draws his settled principle, that signs are perverted and nullified unless they are taken to be visible doctrine. Wesley says the same briefly: the motion or stay of the cloud is fitly called the command of God, because it signified His will and their duty.
19:
The lengths of the halts are set out with a deliberate untidiness. Keil lists the possibilities the text names — many days, or a few, or only from evening till morning and up again at daybreak, or a day and a night, or two days, or a month, or simply days, a space not precisely determined — and holds that the elaboration, abounding as it does with repetitions, is meant to bring out the importance of the fact. On the longest term Ellicott raises a question of date: the word behind a year is literally days, and if the received rendering is right, as he thinks it probably is, these words cannot have been written until after the first arrival at Kadesh, and probably not until the wanderings were over. Gill collects what the Jewish authorities made of the longest terms, the Targum reading the year as a full year and Maimonides reporting eighteen years in one place, with others saying nineteen at Kadesh-barnea. Clarke draws the plain inference, that they were directed in all their peregrinations by the divine counsel alone.

What it meant to keep the charge of the Lord is disputed between two readings. Ellicott allows either sense: it may imply that they were to engage in acts of religious worship, or it may denote adherence to the divine commands and ordinances at large. Calvin names the first of these and rejects it. Some, he says, extend the phrase too far, supposing that when the cloud tarried the people were at leisure and employed themselves in worship; he restricts it instead to the heedfulness which the passage praises at such length. To keep the charge is to regard the will of God with the greatest earnestness and care, for once the cloud had settled they knew they were to stay, but if on the next day they were inattentive it might vanish, and their own negligence would deprive them of an incomparable advantage. Ellicott reaches the same practical result from the clause about the cloud rising by day or by night: there must have been sentinels constantly watching through the night as well as the day, whose office was to give notice the moment it was removed.

The closing verse is read by everyone as a commendation of the people. Gill observes that they rested at command though the place were ever so disagreeable, and journeyed at command though they could have liked to stay; and that a nation otherwise obstinate and perverse, desirous above all of reaching the land of promise, were in this matter submissive in all their stations and journeys. Calvin takes the praise as falling equally on both halves, so that the passage condemns the absurd activity which engages itself in endless work, as if men could only obey God by turmoil, whereas it is sometimes no less a virtue to rest when it so pleases Him. Clarke finds in the whole arrangement an argument as well as a lesson: there could be no trick or imposture here, for Moses, had he been the most cunning of men, could never have imitated these appearances; and God chose to keep the people so dependent upon Himself that He would not even give them regular times of marching or resting, so that they were ever ready to move while wholly ignorant when the summons would come. He turns it directly on the reader, who is a tenant at will to God Almighty and knows neither the hour nor the manner of his own call into the eternal world. Wesley closes on the same note of committal, taking the guidance of the cloud as a figure of the guidance of the Spirit, and putting the fit answer into the reader's mouth: what Thou wilt, and where Thou wilt, only let me be Thine and always in the way of my duty.
